title: Car Fleet
description: Count how many car fleets arrive at a destination by sorting positions and comparing arrival times with a stack.

data.text: There are `n` cars on a single-lane road, all heading to the same destination at `target`. Car `i` starts at `position[i]` with `speed[i]`. A faster car that catches a slower one cannot pass it and joins it as a fleet, travelling at the slower speed from then on. Return the number of fleets that arrive.

**Input:** `target = 12`, `position = [10, 8, 0, 5, 3]`, `speed = [2, 4, 1, 1, 3]`

**Output:** `3`

**Explanation:** The car at 10 arrives at 1, the car at 8 arrives at 1 (they merge), the cars at 5 and 3 arrive at 7 and 3, and the car at 0 arrives at 12.

A car's arrival time ignoring other cars is `(target - position) / speed`. Process the cars from closest-to-target backwards. A car forms a **new** fleet if it would arrive strictly *later* than the fleet ahead of it (it never catches up); otherwise it joins that fleet and inherits the fleet's arrival time.

data.title: Sort by position, scan backwards — O(n log n)
data.content: Only arrival times matter once a car is behind a slower one.

data.title: Compare times, not distances
data.text: It is tempting to simulate positions over time, but the only thing that decides merging is arrival time. Two cars merge exactly when the one behind has an arrival time **less than or equal to** the one ahead. Working in arrival-time space removes the need to model acceleration boundaries.

data.title: Why float comparison is acceptable here
data.text: Arrival times are ratios of small integers with distinct values in the given constraints, so plain `>` is safe. If inputs were adversarial, compare exactly using cross-multiplication of the underlying integers instead.

The same algorithm can be expressed with a stack: push arrival times from the back, popping smaller-or-equal values, and the final stack size is the fleet count. This makes the monotonic-stack connection explicit.

data.title: Same algorithm with an explicit stack
data.content: The stack ends up holding one arrival time per fleet.

data.caption: Fleets form left to right but are counted right to left: a car joins the fleet ahead only when its arrival time is not later.

data.title: Complete solution
data.content: Converting 'will these collide?' into 'what is each one's arrival time?' is the reusable move. The same transformation underpins 'burst balloons' and scheduling problems where the ordering of events matters more than their geometry.
